strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to inform training decisions. Decomposing loss by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective.

The experiments cover dense models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, multiple validation distributions, and additional GPT-NeoX and MoE architectures. This provides meaningful evidence for the observed loss patterns.

Figures 3 and 5 evaluate predictions of subsequent training losses using only early checkpoints, providing stronger evidence than full-trajectory fitting alone. The method substantially improves over the three reported forecasting baselines.

The data-mixture experiment demonstrates potential practical value: the selected mixtures improve final perplexity in all four model/dataset settings and benchmark performance in 12 of 14 comparisons. Architecture tables, package versions, and prediction pseudocode also help document the approach.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the benefit of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor incorporates a piecewise functional form, the known cosine schedule, and boundary constraints, whereas the aggregate-loss baselines lack these features. After a0 and a1 are frozen, the predicted aggregate loss is simply a constant plus a cosine. A comparable aggregate predictor using the same schedule information and functional flexibility is essential to establish the claimed advantage.

The positioning and generality claims exceed the evidence. Kaplan et al. (2020) already investigate training learning curves, and the cited Luo et al. (2025) directly addresses loss prediction across learning-rate schedules but is not compared experimentally. The GPT-NeoX, MoE, and linear-schedule extensions primarily demonstrate full-trajectory fits; they do not establish equivalent forecasting reliability. The linear-schedule experiment also changes the functional form after observing that setting.

The practical selection evidence remains limited. The 10B-token selection point is only 2.5% of training, earlier than the 10–40% prefixes evaluated in the main forecasting experiments. Predicted versus actual candidate rankings and selection uncertainty are not reported. Perplexity improvements are small, such as 8.65 to 8.58 and 7.55 to 7.50 on ID-Val, without independent-run uncertainty. Averaging the last five checkpoints does not substitute for independent repetitions.

Important reproduction details are missing: the outlier-removal threshold, nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation frequency, and actual candidate/selected mixture weights. No implementation or loss-trajectory release is linked. Algorithm 1 also applies calibration when Npred <= Nsep, contradicting the prose and Eq. (15), which require observations after the separation point. These omissions matter because extrapolation depends on the fitted transition and early-curve derivatives.

The theoretical interpretations need qualification. Eq. (17) follows from manually freezing a0 and a1 in Eq. (8); it is a conditional property of the fitted model. The observed approximately uniform loss decreases support a descriptive finding, but neither they nor three suppression experiments establish that positional reweighting is generally unnecessary. Appendix C also incorrectly excludes exponential fits by setting their additive offset to zero, although an offset exponential can have a positive limiting loss.

There is a material inconsistency in the baseline evidence: page 5 states that power-law position fits achieve R² < 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, while Table 9 reports R² > 0.95 for 67% of checkpoints on the 58M ID setting. This needs reconciliation. Together with the missing matched comparison and reproduction details, it prevents a clear Findings recommendation despite the promising empirical results.
